An uncertain nuclear effects model

P(missy) is a nuclear effects model that carries its uncertainty instead of rounding it off. The numbers these calculations run on are ranges in their own sources and single values by the time they reach a conclusion. This one keeps them as ranges, all the way through, and computes what the weapon burns as well as what it destroys. Madeline Berzak

Hi! I’m Madeline, but everyone calls me Maddie. I’m based in Chicago, where I lead the nuclear risk research program at the University of Chicago Existential Risk Lab.

p(missy) came out of what I can only describe as a very large mind map: two years of small insights and loose threads from conversations, finally pinned to one page. What I kept noticing was that nuclear winter never enters the conversation about targeting, and that the parameters the field runs on come from a book published in 1977. Blast physics has not changed. What has changed is how much we know about everything downstream of it, and we still flatten complex systems and uncertain ranges into single point estimates that leave most of that complexity out. I think that pushes the field away from the longer-term consequences of nuclear risk, nuclear winter among them.

I built p(missy) because uncertainty belongs in the conversation, and because nothing existed that made it legible to experts and non-experts at once.

Enjoy it, and tell me what you think. I am always after feedback, at mberzak@uchicago.edu.

– Maddie <3

About (missy)

Every input to a targeting calculation is a range, not a number.

P(missy) is an uncertain nuclear effects model. Rather than solving the standard targeting math once with every input fixed at a single value, it evaluates that same math right across the range each input actually occupies, so that what comes back is a spread of answers rather than one.

The parameters it models are the familiar ones, lethal radius, SSPK (single shot probability of kill), p(miss) and p(kill), and they are the numbers behind force posture analysis, research on weapons effects, and much of what is understood about operational planning. They are what an analyst reaches for in asking whether a counterforce strike could work, how much of an arsenal would survive one, and what an exchange of that kind would cost in lives. P(missy) does not alter any of those formulas; what it shows is how much of the resulting answer was decided by assumptions rather than by physics, which is something a single number can never disclose.

Those inputs are also less settled than they appear, and in one case more settled. The 1,500 to 5,000 psi band quoted for a hardened silo circulates widely and I have not been able to find a locator for it in any of the sources listed here; what is actually on the record is narrower, 2,000 to 3,000. Wartime reliability is somewhere above 0.8 and nobody who says so can tell you where above, and accuracy is a design specification rather than a measurement of anything that has ever been done in anger. The convention is to take a value from the middle of each of those ranges and carry it forward as though it had been settled all along.

Carrying the ranges instead moves the answer. For hardness, accuracy, reliability and yield it moves one way, because the chance of a miss is raised to the number of warheads assigned to each target: averaging across those ranges leaves more silos standing than running the middle of them does. Two of the terms do not obey that rule, and a range that sits off-centre about its own set value can run the other way, which is what the defaults here do. The direction is a property of the input, not a law. The gap widens as the ranges widen either way, and it falls on precisely the question counterforce analysis exists to answer, which is whether the other side would have anything left to retaliate with.

A second argument runs underneath all of this. The fight over counterforce and countervalue targeting is conducted almost entirely on the fallout ledger, counting who dies downwind of a silo field, while fire is the mechanism that actually puts soot in the stratosphere, and nobody adds the two ledgers on the same page. I think the risk of a nuclear winter belongs inside targeting calculations. It isn't in them yet.

What current models miss

What the models we use actually account for.

This is not a complaint that models are simplified, since every model is, and simplifying is most of what makes one usable. The claim is narrower than that. The three tools the field relies on take almost entirely disjoint sets of inputs, and not one of them carries uncertainty from one stage through to the next. Most of the terms in the lower block of the table appear in none of them at all, and two of those rows — fuel load by land use, and firestorm as a probability rather than a yes or no — are empty for p(missy) as well. The NUKEMAP and p(missy) columns can be checked against the tools themselves; the other two are a reading of the published method, which is why this is a table rather than an argument.

Push yield and height of burst down and fallout casualties fall dramatically, which is the standard counterforce result and the reason planners reach for small, accurate weapons rather than large ones. Those same two settings also govern the thermal pulse, and with it how much of the ground below catches fire, so one of these ledgers is counted with real care while the other is not counted at all.

The Effects of Nuclear Weapons

Our understanding is built on a book from 1977.

Samuel Glasstone and Philip Dolan compiled The Effects of Nuclear Weapons for the Departments of Defense and Energy, and the third edition from 1977 has been the reference for blast physics and thermal dynamics ever since. Most of p(missy)'s numbers come out of it. The field still uses many of the visual graphs in Glasstone and Dolan to determine the optimal height of burst (how high to detonate a nuclear weapon) that achieves a certain amount of overpressure to properly destroy a target.

It is a dense book and it is still the one the field runs on. What it cannot account for is everything downstream of the blast that has changed since 1977, which is where the uncertainty in the nuclear winter chain actually lives.

The physical processes have not changed. What goes wrong is downstream of them, when an assumption hardens into doctrine and a range is carried forward as a single standardised data point. Three of those are below.

Three assumptions

Each one is a range the field collapsed into a single number. Click on a panel to open an assumption.

Atmospheric transmittance is the fraction of the fireball’s thermal radiation that survives the path to the target: how much light gets through the air without being absorbed or scattered out of the beam. How far the pulse reaches therefore depends on whether the day is clear, overcast, humid, hazy, foggy or raining. That distance sets the radius of the circle inside which things catch fire, and that circle, taken with how much combustible material is standing in it, is what the estimates of how much burns and whether a firestorm forms are built on.

Glasstone and Dolan do not ignore transmittance. They compute it, and the transmittance values used below are theirs. What they hold fixed is the weather: the curves, and the worked examples built on them, assume one condition throughout, a cloudless day with about 12 miles of visibility, which they take as typical of a clear day over a city. That is the simplification worth arguing with. Weather on the day of a strike is not a known quantity, and the difference between a clear day and a foggy one is the difference between a third of a city's fuel igniting and most of it.

Under review. Two things about the numbers below are being checked against the book rather than asserted here. Entry 02 reads the values 0.9 and 0.3 off Fig. 7.42 and presents them as clear weather against fog, with 0.6 interpolated between them; this page inherited that reading. A reviewer working from the 1977 edition (entry 06) reads Fig. 7.42 instead as radiant exposure against slant range, drawn at one fixed visibility, with the transmittance curves at Fig. 7.98 — where τ falls from about 0.9 close to the burst to under 0.1 at thirty kilometres on a single day, because the further light travels the more of it is scattered or absorbed. If that reading is right then these are real Glasstone and Dolan numbers put on the wrong axis: a range over distance, presented as a range over weather. The same reviewer reads τ = 1.0 as appearing in the book only as the opening guess in an iterative calculation and for bursts high enough that there is barely any air in the path, rather than as a standing default.

Which reading is right changes what the figures below are evidence of, but not that the spread matters, and not the arithmetic: at a fixed τ the ignited area is linear in τ, so the 67% below is just one minus 0.3 over 0.9. It is flagged here rather than quietly corrected because settling it needs the book open at both figures. Water vapour, carbon dioxide and other aerosols also absorb selectively by wavelength, so transmittance is a function of the spectrum as well as of the distance. The equation, and where its constant comes from, is written out on the model page under Fire.

What Glasstone and Dolan hold fixed is not transmittance but the weather: the curves, and the worked examples built on them, assume one clear day. The field has carried that assumption forward ever since without restating it.

The ignition threshold is the amount of heat a material has to absorb before it catches fire, measured as thermal fluence in calories per square centimetre. Glasstone and Dolan put the working figure at about 10 cal/cm², and that single number is what sets the ignition radius. For a 15 kiloton airburst like Hiroshima, 10 cal/cm² is reached about 2.04 km out with no atmosphere in the way, giving roughly 13 km². Every estimate built on the Hiroshima proxy starts from that circle. But the book's own tables run from 4 cal/cm² to 24 at 35 kilotons and from 11 to 50 at 20 megatons, which is a factor of six across materials and another two across yields, and the number carried forward is one value taken out of that.

There is a second problem, which is that the threshold is not a property of the material alone. It also depends on how fast the heat arrives. A fixed threshold assumes the energy is delivered instantaneously, and it is not: the thermal pulse of a 1 kiloton airburst lasts about 0.4 seconds, while a 10 megaton explosion takes more than 20 seconds to deliver its energy. Slower delivery gives heat time to conduct away before the surface reaches ignition temperature, so thick wood, wet materials and dense plastics all need more energy from a big weapon than they would from a small one. Glasstone and Dolan say as much themselves. The threshold rises with yield, and the models built on their work still use one number for every weapon.

Bigger weapons also shade themselves. Neither of the next two numbers is a cited result; both are my own reasoning about what the timing and the geometry imply, and I have not found either of them measured. In a 20 second pulse, the fires that start in the first five seconds put up smoke that shields the edge of the target area for the remaining fifteen, and surface bursts loft enough debris to cut the fluence arriving further out by something like 20 to 40% compared to a cleaner airburst. A static circle is being used to describe something that unfolds over time.

Fuel load is the amount of combustible material standing in a given target area, and the rate at which it burns. Hiroshima in 1945 was built almost entirely of wood, almost nothing above two storeys, and confined to a compact area. A modern city is not. New York, Chicago and Los Angeles are reinforced concrete, structural steel and plate glass at the centre, and the centre runs out through suburbs, parks and industrial corridors rather than stopping. The plastics inside the buildings, and the rest of the interior contents, burn too, and they are not in the 1945 figure either.

A target list and relative nuclear winter risk constructed upon 1940s urban morphology is making an implicit bet about the atmosphere, and that bet belongs inside the targeting calculation rather than downstream of it. Which way the bet runs is not settled either. Concrete and steel are harder to set alight than the wood of 1945, while the plastics inside them give off two to three times more soot per unit mass than wood does (entry 02), and those two facts pull in opposite directions.

Ignition radius at three transmittances · 15 kt airburst

The three transmittances are read off Fig. 7.42 by entry 02, which takes 0.9 and 0.3 and interpolates 0.6 between them. Whether those are Glasstone and Dolan's numbers at all, whether that is the right figure, and whether the range is one over weather or one over distance, is the open question set out above.

Excellent visibility, clear day τ ≈ 0.9 r = √( fYτ / 4πQ ) r = √( 0.35 × 15 × 1012 × 0.9 / 4π × 10 ) r ≈ 1.94 km area = π(1.94)² ≈ 11.8 km²
Moderate visibility, hazy τ ≈ 0.6 r = √( fYτ / 4πQ ) r = √( 0.35 × 15 × 1012 × 0.6 / 4π × 10 ) r ≈ 1.58 km area = π(1.58)² ≈ 7.8 km²
Poor visibility, fog or rain τ ≈ 0.3 r = √( fYτ / 4πQ ) r = √( 0.35 × 15 × 1012 × 0.3 / 4π × 10 ) r ≈ 1.12 km area = π(1.12)² ≈ 3.9 km²

f is the thermal fraction of yield, Y the yield in calories, Q the ignition threshold in cal/cm², and τ the atmospheric transmittance: the fraction of the fireball’s thermal radiation that survives the path to the target, which is what visibility measures. Between clear air and fog the ignited area falls by 67%, which is where that figure comes from. Holding τ constant across the whole radius, as these three cases do, is itself a simplification: on any real day it falls with distance. The Fire tab does it the other way round, setting the visibility and letting τ fall as the light travels, which is closer to how Glasstone and Dolan handle it. The equation for τ, and where its constant comes from, is written out on the model page under Fire.

How to use the model Carrying the uncertainty Case study

How to use the model

The model reproduces a worked example, and then you widen it.

It opens on a case taken out of a targeting briefing: a W78 warhead at 335 kilotons and 120 metre accuracy, aimed at a silo hardened to 3,000 psi, two warheads to each silo and two hundred silos in the set. Run it as it stands and it returns the figures the briefing does. The Checks tab tests every one of them against results already in print, every time the page loads, and says so plainly if any of them drift.

Where to start

  1. Open One target and read the steps from the top down. That column is the standard method, taken apart: a lethal radius, a damage function, where the warhead lands, and the chance the target survives what is aimed at it. The last row is the number a briefing reports.
  2. Look at the three figures above the steps. The first is the chance one warhead kills the target, the second is the chance the target survives all of them, and the third is what happens to the second once every input is allowed the range its own sources give it. The distance between the second and the third is what the model exists to show.
  3. Now pick a different target and a different weapon from the two menus at the top of the panel. Each one sets a value and a span, both taken from the source named beside it. A weapon is not a number; it is a number with a footnote, and the footnote is what changes the answer.
  4. Widen a span by hand. Every control on the panel carries one: a value on the slider and a range underneath it in the same unit. The spans a target arrives with are the ones its own source supports, which for a silo's hardness is narrower than most people expect. Widen one past that and run it again. Nothing about the physics has changed; only the claim about what is known has, and the page will now be showing you the consequences of a number nobody has published.
  5. Go to Equations, not one equation, which does the same thing to the formula itself rather than to what is fed into it. Untick two of the lethal radius expressions so only one is in play, run it, and put them all back. The gap between those two runs is the part of the answer that comes from nothing but a choice of published equation.
  6. Move to Target set, where the same answer is carried out to a field. Read What each input is worth first: it sorts the inputs by how far each one moves the answer on its own, and that ordering is usually the most useful thing on the page.

What each input means

The panel is the equation. Its groups are the groups in p(kill; target | weapon | delivery | environment), in that order, and every control on it is one named term. Five terms carry a label saying named, not computed: those are the ones this model can name but does not evaluate, and they are on the panel rather than left off it so that the size of the omission stays visible.

Hardness, H
The blast overpressure a target absorbs before it stops working, in pounds per square inch. Lieber and Press run a modern intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) silo at 3,000 and bracket one at roughly 2,000 to 3,000; Davis and Schilling give 300 for a Minuteman silo before the hardening programme and 900 after it. The 2 to 5 psi usually quoted for a road-mobile launcher or an ordinary house is widely repeated and, as far as I can find, not in any of the sources listed here.
Damage function width, σD
How fast the chance of destroying the target falls off across the lethal radius. At 0 it is the cookie cutter every published formula assumes. At 0.20 it is the Sigma-20 curve Davis and Schilling name and then decline to use.
Footprint, A
Zero for a silo, which is a point. Not zero for an apron, a garrison or a dispersal area, where a warhead landing anywhere on the footprint is on top of the target. This is the term that lets the model leave silos.
Yield, Y
The energy released, in kilotons. Hiroshima was about 15, and the W78 on a Minuteman III is 335. The same yield drives the fire calculation on the third tab.
Warheads on this target, n
The exponent. Assign more than one and the target survives only if every one of them misses, which is where the whole convexity argument comes from.
Height of burst
Only the Brode and Small pressure field reads it. Leave it above zero and switch formulas to watch all three stop responding to an input that matters.
CEP
A containment radius: draw a circle of this radius on the aim point and half the warheads land inside it. It is a 50% localisation region, not a one-sigma figure and not a bound. The familiar 68% belongs to one axis at a time; the circle of radius one σ holds about 39%, and it takes about 1.3 CEP to reach 70%.
Shape of the error, σdr/σcr
The C in CEP stands for circular and the real error is an ellipse, longer along the line of flight than across it. This is the ratio of the two, with CEP held fixed as it moves. Nothing in the open literature gives this ratio for a deployed system, which is exactly why it is a control here rather than a buried assumption.
Aiming bias, b
A systematic offset of the whole pattern from the target: guidance calibration, accumulated gravity model error, or a target whose surveyed coordinates are wrong. Unlike CEP it does not average out over many shots or over many targets, which is why it is carried separately.
Reliability, ρ
The share of warheads that arrive and go off. The span is the two values Lieber and Press themselves use: 0.80, which they call the traditional baseline and run their headline rows on, and 0.90, which they call realistic and use in rows 4 to 7.
Fratricide, q
The chance an earlier burst takes out a later warhead aimed at the same target. Arrivals are seconds apart and debris persists, so the first two are unaffected and the risk starts at the third. At 0 it is the independent case every published formula assumes.
Targets in the set, N
How many targets are being attacked. Two hundred is roughly a silo field. Set it to 1 to read the calculation for a single target, with no counting at all.
Yield exponent
How lethal radius scales with yield. Every formula here uses the cube root, 0.3333, which follows from peak overpressure alone. A silo is damaged by how long the pressure lasts as well as how high it climbs, and a bigger weapon holds it longer, so cube-root scaling understates a megaton-class warhead. Davis and Schilling's note 11 works back from Wohlstetter's figures to 0.3690, anchored at 50 kt.
Lethal radius formula
Which published expression the steps use. It is set to the General Electric calculator, the one the standard exchange arithmetic inherited, so the single answer stays comparable to what a briefing reports.
Formulas the quadrature draws from
Which expressions the ranges are carried across. Davis and Schilling print four readings of lethal radius, all fitted to the same test data, and at five megatons against a 300 psi target they return anything from 3,762 to 4,095 feet. That disagreement is an uncertainty like any other, and there is no reason it should be the one input a model treats as settled.
Points
How finely the box of input ranges is covered. There is no seed and no run-to-run variation: the point set is a lattice, so the same inputs give the same answer every time. The convergence line reports what the last doubling moved.

What comes back

Inputs as set
One pass with every input fixed where its slider sits. This is the number a briefing reports, and it is the thing the rest of the page is measured against.
Spread from chance alone
What you get if the odds themselves were known exactly and only the coin was uncertain. This is the error bar usually quoted alongside a result, and it is the smaller of the two.
Spread once the ranges are carried
The average across the whole box of input ranges, with a 95% band. Nearly always the largest of the three. Which side of the single answer it falls on depends on the input: see the reading under the figure.
What each input is worth
One bar per input, each running from the answer at one end of that input's range to the answer at the other, so the longest bar is the input the answer depends on most. The values printed under the ends of a bar are the input values that produce them, which is where the direction is legible. The ticks inside a bar are at equal steps of the input, so evenly spaced ticks mean an even trade and bunched ticks mean the middle of that range is not a fair summary of it.
One hundred attacks
A hundred outcomes read off the distribution at even intervals, stacked over the number of targets each one left standing. They are read off rather than drawn, so nothing in the picture clusters by accident.
Worth holding on toOne target here means one aim point rather than one warhead, and a surviving silo may hold a missile with multiple independently targetable re-entry vehicles (MIRV) carrying several of them, so the number of surviving targets is a floor on surviving warheads rather than a count of them. That error runs in the same direction as the convexity gap does, which is toward understating what the other side would have left to retaliate with.

Carrying the uncertainty

The method was invented for this exact problem, in the same laboratory.

The idea is to answer a question you cannot pin the numbers down for. Rather than solving the problem once with a single value for each input, you solve it over and over across the range each input could plausibly occupy. What happens to the answer if the accuracy is a little worse, the silo a little harder, the weather a little foggier? What comes back is not an answer but a distribution of answers, and the shape of that distribution is exactly what a single calculation cannot tell you.

The method and the subject grew up together. Stanislaw Ulam arrived at the modern version of it at Los Alamos in 1946, while recovering from an illness and playing solitaire. He wanted to know the odds that a hand of Canfield would come out, found the combinatorics tedious, and realised he could lay out a hundred hands and count the wins instead. The problem he actually needed it for was neutron diffusion in a weapon core, which had plenty of data and no way to be solved on paper. John von Neumann carried the idea to the ENIAC, Nicholas Metropolis supplied the name, and the first fully automated Monte Carlo calculation, in the spring of 1948, was of a fission core.

Castle Bravo is what it looks like when a range gets collapsed into a single number. Detonated at Bikini Atoll on 1 March 1954, it was predicted at 6 megatons and delivered 15. The predicted range was really 4 to 8 megatons, and some of the designers had cautioned that the yield could reach 15, but 6 was the figure that travelled. The error underneath it was one assumption: the lithium-7 in the fuel, about 60% of the lithium content, was treated as inert, and it was not. It produced tritium instead, and that tritium fused. The largest weapon the United States has ever detonated came in at two and a half times its design yield, eight years after Monte Carlo was invented in the same laboratory, because one number in the calculation was carried forward as though it were settled.

So the case for carrying a range rather than assuming a value is neither new nor abstract. What is strange is that the targeting math downstream of the weapon never took the method up. Force posture analysis is still done overwhelmingly at the middle of every range and reported as a single figure, even though the tool for doing otherwise was built in the same place, for the same reason, and is now cheap enough to run in a browser tab.

Why it suits this problem

  1. The math is cheap. One pass through lethal radius, SSPK, reliability and p(miss) takes a fraction of a millisecond, so a few thousand passes take well under a second. There was never a computational reason to avoid doing this, only a question of patience.
  2. Averaging the inputs is not the same as averaging the answers. p(miss) raised to the number of warheads is a convex function, which means the answer taken from the middle of every range sits systematically below the average of the answers across those ranges. Carrying the range is the only way to see that gap, and no amount of care with a single calculation will reveal it.
  3. What is worth reporting is a distribution. Anyone who needs to know the risk that twenty silos survive rather than one is asking about the tail of a curve, and a point estimate does not have a tail.

Why this model no longer rolls dice

Everything above is an argument for carrying the range. It is not an argument for drawing random numbers, and version 5 of this model stopped doing that.

Look at what is actually being asked for. The average of p(kill) across a set of input ranges is an integral over a box: up to eleven dimensions wide — ten input spans and the choice of formula — and seven at the defaults, with a smooth integrand and known edges. Pseudorandom sampling is a way of doing that integral, and by modern standards a poor one. Its error falls as one over the square root of the number of draws, it clusters and leaves gaps because that is what random numbers do, and it makes the answer depend on a seed, so a result cannot be quoted without quoting the seed alongside it.

What this model uses instead is a rank-1 lattice: a deterministic point set spread evenly through the box by construction, generated from the plastic constant in as many dimensions as there are ranges. On this integrand, measured against a reference run, its error at 4,096 points runs about twelve times below the average error of pseudorandom sets of the same size on the six spans the defaults carry, and about five times with all ten spans open; the figure is reported on the Method tab rather than re-run on every page load. There is no seed. There is no run-to-run variation. Two people who set the same inputs get the same answer to the last digit printed, which for a method meant to audit other people's numbers is not a nicety.

The change is also worth making for what it says. A simulation invites the reading that the model is generating scenarios, rolling for outcomes, playing the war out. It is not, and it never was. It is evaluating one function across the range of inputs the literature actually supports and reporting the range of answers that come out. Calling that quadrature rather than simulation is the more accurate description of what is happening, and the more honest one about how much is being claimed.

Two things follow from it on the page. The counting that happens after the integral — how many of two hundred targets survive, given the odds for one — is closed form and is not sampled at all. What is still approximate is the spread of the odds themselves, which comes from the quadrature. And a field of targets with different hardnesses is now spread evenly across its span rather than drawn from it, which is why nothing in the figures clusters by chance any more. It used to, and the clustering looked like it meant something.

What it does not doNone of this invents information. If the ranges going in are wrong, the distribution coming out is wrong with more decimal places attached. The method carries uncertainty through a calculation; it does not reduce it. Every range in the panel is a judgement, taken from the open literature where the literature has one, and marked in gold where it does not.

Where to read more

  1. Eckhardt, Roger. “Stan Ulam, John von Neumann, and the Monte Carlo Method.” Los Alamos Science 15, Special Issue (1987): 131–41. mcnp.lanl.gov.

    • The origin story, the solitaire hand, and von Neumann's letter proposing the ENIAC calculation. Also the clearest short explanation of what a random number generator has to do, and why that is harder than it sounds.

  2. Metropolis, Nicholas. “The Beginning of the Monte Carlo Method.” Los Alamos Science 15, Special Issue (1987): 125–30.

    • The companion piece, by the man who named the method, on how it was actually run on the machines of the late 1940s.

  3. Metropolis, Nicholas, and S. Ulam. “The Monte Carlo Method.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 44, no. 247 (1949): 335–41. doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1949.10483310.

    • The first unclassified paper on the method and the first to carry the name. Six pages, and readable.

  4. National Security Archive. “Castle BRAVO at 70: The Worst Nuclear Test in U.S. History.” Briefing Book, February 29, 2024. nsarchive.gwu.edu.

    • The declassified record behind the yield figures above, including the General Advisory Committee minutes giving the predicted yield as four to eight megatons, and Carson Mark's explanation that lithium-7 had been assumed to be a much less good fuel than lithium-6.

Case study

dismantling the illusion of certainty in targeting, cccr 2026, and a p(missy) targeting case study on lieber and press (2017)

In short

Lieber and Press argue that the accuracy revolution has severed the link between disarming an adversary and killing millions of civilians, and they test and demonstrate this argument with two strikes against the same five hardened sites in North Korea. It is the load-bearing claim for why modern counterforce is more humane — so, I rebuilt it all in p(missy) to see what changes, if anything. The more “humane” strike option is only humane when everything lands exactly where it is supposed to; the perceived “success” is dependent on which accuracy figure we choose to believe.

thinking about nuclear winter

In Whole World on Fire, Lynn Eden debunks the long-held assumption that blast physics is predictable while fire damage is not. Eden concludes that this is less of a technical problem and more of an organizational (people) one: knowledge-laden routines are solutions to problems that organizations decide to solve (Eden, 2004). Fire damage is just as predictable as blast damage but no one was motivated to predict it during the Cold War. While I agree with Eden that these problems are organizational and sociological, I argue they are also deeply epistemological and cultural. These “solutions,” however harmless they may seem on the surface, harden over time and deeply influence how current knowledge gaps are addressed.

Lynn Eden published Whole World on Fire in 2004, at the height of the nuclear winter modeling hiatus period. While Eden’s work in many ways became a classic, sparking important conversations at the time, there is only so much one book can do to erode a decades long norm. Most of our considerations stop at the moment of nuclear use, and never cross over to the post-detonation domain. Eden also asserts that the field never built the routine to include fire damage considerations into targeting and nuclear risk. Once a “routine” is missing for long enough, it stops looking like a real gap and starts looking like the hard edge of the discipline; a boundary we need not go past. Blast physics are within this manufactured boundary, while fire rests outside of it but no one remembers why.

This choice (or, lack thereof) was in a way a very rational one: as decision-makers and the public demanded certainty on nuclear risk that informed resilience and civil defense, but also nuclear strategy and targeting. In Prisoners of Reason, Sonja Amadae’s broader argument says that rational choice formalisms often carry normative commitments, even if we are unable to see them on the surface (Amadae, 2016). Collapsing an uncertain range to a point estimate and communicating it as certain, is a decision about which consequences count, and which ones don’t.

A nuclear winter is a sudden cooling climate effect that is a result of black carbon and soot being lofted into the lower stratosphere post-nuclear detonation, where it remains for some long-ish indefinite amount of time. A nuclear winter would be, for a lack of better words, very bad. One of the key factors in our understanding of nuclear winter risk, are firestorms: self-sustaining convection column of fire that sometimes has enough force to push soot, black carbon, and other particulate up into the atmosphere. If the firestorm is too weak, the soot may settle in the troposphere and rain out, but if the firestorm is strong enough, soot will be injected into the stratosphere causing a nuclear winter effect.

I heard some experts talking at one point about how countervalue (targeting an adversary’s cities and what they value) targeting may be a stronger deterrent (partly à cause d’ “ease”… less accuracy needed), and after nuclear winter was brought up in the discussion, one of them said, “We had over 100 tests in the pacific and there was no nuclear winter from any of those, so it doesn’t matter.” Atmospheric tests over the Pacific ocean can’t trigger a nuclear winter, as there is not enough combustible material to cause a firestorm, let alone any combustible material at all. This is sort of bonkers but also a little alarming, especially after decades of nuclear winter research that tells us (1) nuclear winter is a big risk, (2) firestorms are central to that risk, and (3) we don’t understand everything. It feels irresponsible to not understand something that is downstream of all the strategic debates we consider. Our understanding of nuclear winter is not only one event, but a chain of complex mechanisms: thermal ignition, material fuel load, firestorm behavior, soot injection, and global circulation. Uncertainties that remain early in the mechanism chain multiply as each event builds upon the previous ones.

I think about nuclear winter a lot. In fact, I think about it almost everyday. Somewhat ironically, I guess this isn’t typical in my line of work. I’d argue that much of the nuclear field ought to contemplate nuclear winter more often than they currently do. At the end of the day, nuclear winter is the catastrophic consequence we seek to prevent and it thus should underscore all of our debates and analysis. This meta-reflection along with many other disjointed thoughts formed the basis of my first expert panel talk at the Cambridge Conference on Catastrophic Risks with CSER at Magdalene College, University of Cambridge on September 17. Speaking alongside Mette Eilstrup-Sangiovanni, S.M. Amadae, and James Acton, I argued that leaving nuclear winter out of targeting analysis pushes the analyst further away from existential stakes, and that uncertain ranges belong in our discussions. In this culture, innocent simplifications and estimates often become analogous to certainty over time.

about p(missy): an uncertain nuclear effects model

P(missy) is an uncertain nuclear effects model I built with the help of Claude to visualize the organizational gap Eden identified in her research. It is a model that accounts for a range of uncertainties in simulating target lethality and weapons effects that significantly affect results, and thus, analysis. These uncertainties are most often flattened into vast simplifications and single point estimates, only reflecting a small slice of the complex reality. I talked about an early version of p(missy) in my Sandia recap post, but the model has advanced significantly since then as I’ve refined the structure, inputs, and interface. This model emerged, like many projects of mine do, from a convergence of hundreds of tiny thoughts and ideas on the things we choose to leave out of our analysis and decision-making, as well as where our assumptions remain unquestioned.

While the blast physics and parameters remain the same, problems in analysis occur when these assumptions form and harden into doctrine: when a range is collapsed into a single standardized data point. Problems and risks multiply over time when these assumptions are not questioned and the risk landscape shifts. The nuclear field still references Glasstone and Dolan’s The Effects of Nuclear Weapons from 1977 in all research on counterforce and countervalue targeting, as well as weapons effects. It is so fundamental, in fact, that most of p(missy)’s numbers emerge from it: we still use many of the visual graphs in Glasstone and Dolan to determine the optimal height of burst (how high to detonate a nuclear weapon) that achieves a certain amount of overpressure to properly destroy a target. These parameters codify the organizational blindness described above, turning a complex, uncertain reality into a flattened and largely unquestioned routine. Glasstone and Dolan acknowledge most of the ranges p(missy) expands, but nonetheless default to simplification for the purposes of calculations and estimates. These are some of the terms and parameters the field currently uses to do these calculations:

Despite decades of research on nuclear risk and targeting, those inputs are also far less settled than they appear. A hardened silo sits somewhere between 1,500 and 5,000 psi depending on which missile silo and whose estimate you take. Wartime reliability is somewhere above ~0.8 and no one who says so can tell you where above, and accuracy is a design specification rather than a measurement of anything that has ever been done in anger. The convention is to take a value from the middle of each of those ranges and carry it forward as though it had been settled all along. We use these simplified formulas (if you could even call them formulas!) in the nuclear field for research and analysis. Public analysis, making use of non-classified and open-source information, often affects policy and informs defense/government decisions. What happens when everything we are producing is uncertain?

I named the model p(missy), because p(miss)—or, probability of miss—is the targeting parameter I had been most familiar with prior to Sandia. More importantly, I think p(miss) highlights that we as a field far too often miss deeper considerations that are hidden below the surface, just like this one. Yield and height of burst determine the probability of kill, but yield and height of burst also determine the ignition radius and inform how much soot is produced: one set of inputs can produce two different nuanced answers.

a p(missy) case study on lieber & press (2017)

Keir Lieber and Daryl Press are best known for the first half of their 2017 paper, “The New Era of Counterforce,” specifically for the argument that accuracy and remote sensing may end the survivability of nuclear forces. The part I am fascinated with is quieter and more subtle, grappling with the dawn of the low-casualty counterforce. Lieber and Press argue that the accuracy revolution has severed the link between disarming an adversary and killing millions of civilians, and they test and demonstrate this argument with two strikes against the same five hardened sites in North Korea.

The high-yield attack employed ten W88 warheads with a 455-kiloton yield, and two warheads against each target. The low-yield attack uses twenty B61 bombs with a 0.3 kiloton yield, set to detonate at an altitude that “maximizes effectiveness while minimizing fallout.” In both scenarios, all five targets are destroyed with 95% certainty, and while in the high-yield option 2-3 million are dead, the low yield option reports fewer than 100 casualties (at target sites). This argument is inherently moral in nature, but the evidence in support of it is quantitative. It is also the load-bearing claim for why modern counterforce is more humane — so, I rebuilt it all in p(missy) to see what changes, if anything.

It is important to note that I am not running a completely different model. Lieber and Press’ lethal radius formula also comes from Davis and Schilling (1973), just like p(missy). Their damage function is also the same as mine, except the spread is set to 0, not accounting for a range. If I set the damage function parameter to 0, the model returns their same published results: their 1985 Minuteman III strike leaves 42 of 200 hardened silos surviving, as does mine. Each subsequent run has the same inputs drawn from uncertain ranges Lieber and Press acknowledged in their paper’s footnotes. After the Minuteman III calibration run, I input the high-yield option parameters from Figure 3, exactly as described: at 455 kilotons, with 2 warheads per each of the 5 targets in the set. P(missy) spits out a 98.4% chance of destroying each one.

Alongside the paper, Lieber and Press also published a technical appendix detailing all of the formulas and methods. The 95% certainty parameter in both the high and low yield attack examples was not actually a result; the appendix explains that instead of starting with hardness and yield and solving forward for probability of kill, they started with the desired probability of kill, input 95% into the fourth formula, and solve backwards to find the accuracy that would produce it (appendix p. 7). The result is ~13 meters. The B61-12 is later described as likely being within reach of that requirement. Solving backwards is an acceptable method for asking what accuracy a weapon would need to destroy a set of targets, though the 95% parameter reappears in Figure 3 of the actual paper as a property of the strike calculation itself. As if somewhere between those pages, a quick simplification evolved into a finding of its own.

I ran the model forward rather than backward in p(missy) using the accuracy figures Lieber and Press cite in their own footnotes: CEP (circular error probable) is ~5 meters with a clean GPS signal, ~30 meters without one, and ~15 meters in the reported B61-12 test drop. At 15 meters, the paper’s claims are still right, and the probability that any of the five target sites survive is ~3%. At 20 meters it increases to 23%, and at 30 meters (their own number for a GPS-denied environment) the disarming strike fails to destroy the target 3 out of 4 times. All of these values are Lieber and Press’ from the paper and technical appendix, and GPS denial in a war with a nuclear-armed adversary is closer to the reality we should expect and plan for.

This analysis feels uncertain, but also sort of lopsided, as the high-yield option presents little change under the same treatment. Everything that constructs the probability of kill, or p(kill), parameter runs through a single ratio: the lethal radius divided by the CEP (or how far the blast reaches set against how far off the warhead is likely to land). A W88 warhead at 455 kilotons has a lethal radius of ~259 meters against a hardened silo and a CEP of ~90; a ratio of nearly 3 to 1. Circular error probable (CEP) is a parameter that measures a particular weapons systems delivery accuracy: the radius of a circle that 1/2 of a big number of identical missiles operating without malfunction would likely land within, reflecting the median rather than mean (MDAA, 2026). A higher CEP indicates more uncertainty and lower weapon system precision.

The ratio between lethal radius and CEP feeds into the single shot probability of kill (SSPK) calculation, the second formula in Lieber and Press’ appendix, where it’s squared and used as an exponent: SSPK=1-0.5^((LR/CEP)^2). This functionally means that once the ratio is large enough, improving accuracy barely changes the output, but when the ratio is small, even a little extra inaccuracy costs a lot more. The W88 warhead’s ratio is almost ~3 to 1 (~259/90), far enough past the point where accuracy doesn’t really matter any longer. On the 0.3 kiloton low-yield option, the ~22 meter lethal radius is smaller than the spread of the accuracy estimates being fed into it. The more “humane” strike option is only humane when everything lands exactly where it is supposed to; the perceived “success” is dependent on which accuracy figure we choose to believe.

While both targeting options were said to have “greater than 95% certainty,” they arrive at this conclusion through different channels. The high-yield strike works basically no matter how accurate the warhead is upon detonation, as the blast area is large enough that landing slightly off doesn’t change much. The low-yield strike, in contrast, only destroys the targets effectively if the bombs are very accurate: this is the uncertain number that is hard to estimate, since it depends on things like whether GPS still works.

The results from p(missy) illustrate that accuracy is the uncertain input that changes the result most drastically, outweighing everything else 17 to 1 for the low-yield option. For the high-yield option, the most uncertain variable becomes reliability, or whether the warhead and delivery system work at all after launch — a problem that is easily solved by increasing the number of warheads per target. Using expanded uncertain ranges rather than single point estimates increases the number of targets likely to survive the attack by ~14x for the low-yield strike, and less than 2x for the high-yield one. A plausibly “disarming” strike that fails is not merely a lesser version of one that succeeds, rather just a plain ol’ strike followed by whatever survives it.

The paper’s height of burst estimate for the low-yield strike option is never stated, returning to my previous discussion on the tendency to default Glasstone and Dolan (1977). Lieber and Press describe height of burst plainly; an altitude that maximizes effectiveness and expands the blast radius, while minimizing radioactive fallout. These strike attributes are dynamic, relying upon height of burst (ground or air). Ground and lower-to-the-ground bursts create more pressure that can more effectively destroy a hardened target like a missile silo, but if the fireball touches the ground, it sucks up dirt and debris that become radioactive fallout. Much of this is dependent on the amount of combustible material and “stuff” within the target area. The ideal altitude Lieber and Press describe is merely a compromise: as low as possible without the fireball reaching the ground, such that one can maximize the overpressure on a target and minimize fallout and firestorms.

The paper’s appendix calculates this with a formula taken directly from Glasstone and Dolan (FT= 180 x W^0.4), which detonates the 0.3 kiloton weapon at ~111 feet. The decision to use an air burst to lower the risk of fallout is simultaneously the decision that increases the thermal fraction (the percent of a nuke’s energy released as heat; a ground burst somewhat loses this to its own dust and debris) from around 0.18 to 0.35. On a clear day, the ignition radius would be about 289 meters. Had they decided a ground burst would be the more effective option, the ignition radius shrinks to around 207 meters, nearly halving the area that could catch fire. As the ignition radius increases, a firestorm can become within reach (depending on fuel load and how much ignites at once), and a firestorm with a high enough force can loft soot past the troposphere. I designed p(missy) with the ability to model targets, but also fire and combustibility which is (still) absent from most debates.

This all harkens back to Lynn Eden’s central thesis in broader, perhaps, more expansive terms: just because a process is complex and uncertain, doesn’t mean we can’t try to understand and predict it within a some specific confidence interval. Fire damage and spread from nuclear detonations is predictable. Her argument has not only remained true, but has over time become epistemically hardened. Eden’s fire damage and predictability argument is mentioned only once in Lieber and Press (2017), in footnote 53 on page 28: “If counterforce targets are located outside cities (as most are), targeters can select aim points, yields, and heights of burst to minimize fire and overpressure consequences for civilians,” (L&P, 2017). The fatality estimates come from HPAC 5.1, a tool built around fallout rather than fire spread, thus, the humane counterforce claim merely rests on one register while the other was never filled in. When Eden’s fire argument is included in research, materials are generalized to a constant 10 cal/cm^2 ignition threshold/radiant exposure for all materials regardless of how they burn.

implications

Conventional wisdom is that purely counterforce targeting strategy largely eliminates the risk of nuclear winter, but this isn’t true. While counterforce is widely understood to mean targeting an adversary’s nuclear forces and nuclear command and control capabilities (targeting an adversary’s means to fight) it still targets other kinds of assets. James Acton has already made a version of this argument: many counterforce targets sit in or near cities, so the collateral damage is a matter of geography (Acton, 2023). I think there is a second version of this that is about math rather than geography, and the two are complementary. While Acton argues the targets are in the wrong place, I argue the same inputs can produce a second answer. A facility like the Peterson Space and Air Force Base in Colorado Springs presents a challenge for targeting, with expansive above ground infrastructure, as well as hardened targets like the Cheyenne Mountain Complex just a few miles southwest, and U.S. Northern Command/NORAD. It is strategic in nature, but it is also massive in scale with a lot of combustible material in what would encompass the target area.

Targeting plans are also structured in strategic phases: in other words, counterforce targeting may still target cities and population centers by proximity to war time industry, and national-level political and military leadership: Washington D.C., is still an urban population center (with a lot of combustible material). The law of war, more formally International Humanitarian Law (IHL), does not hold parties responsible for remote or unforeseeable consequences, although it does require military commanders to take into account “indirect” consequences, if they are reasonably foreseeable (Robinson and Nohle, 2016). Indirect, thus, does not always mean the same thing as long-term.

There are also condition and correlation problems, particularly with the weather that we have to take into account in analysis. Atmospheric transmittance (the fraction of thermal radiation that survives the path to the target) is one of the core inputs that determines how far thermal radiation actually travels, and as a result, the ignition area varies greatly with visibility. Between clear skies, and rain or dense fog, there is an ~87% reduction in ignition area. In an active war with Russia or China, the U.S. can’t sit around and wait until there are perfect blue skies to launch. Under compressed decision timelines, the U.S. would have to launch when it is required. A thermal calculation at a single visibility value (equal to 1: clear skies) isn’t a simplification of the problem, but really an entirely different one (G&D, 1977). Understanding these uncertain ranges can help governments and decision makers understand what nuclear forces can and cannot do, and how these uncertainties widen under conditions that aren’t up to us.

old questions, new considerations

P(missy) was originally just a fun project to help me learn how to use Claude Code; a visualization of many insights and ideas that connected in my mind over the summer to show how uncertain our thinking actually is. As it has evolved, the model has become a methodology of its own beyond just something broadly informative. P(missy) is inherently and outrightly uncertain, and that was intentionally the whole point: the model can help make our analysis more comprehensive by asserting what we do know, and what we still don’t know, preventing us from making across the board assertions that often become assumptions remaining unquestioned. There is immense value in critically examining even the most unpleasant things that govern nuclear risk.

P(missy) and this case study also forces us to consider the question of how many nuclear weapons is actually enough. When designing a nuclear force and thinking about the two peer problem, answers are often delivered as a single number, when all along they should have just been a range. How does this change how we argue about force structure in a tri-polar security landscape? Can we effectively deter with fewer nuclear weapons?

At a more meta-level, this research is downstream of society’s appetite and desire for certainty. The public demands it, and in return experts must provide it, so it makes sense that often times this certainty may not be very well grounded in reality and instead fulfilling other strange and abstract sociocultural purposes. Why does uncertainty have to be such a bad thing? And with that, things end just as they began: with me writing in my office on a rainy afternoon, sipping a cup of earl grey tea and contemplating nuclear winter.

FAQs and applications

FAQs and Applications

p(missy) is an instrument for testing whether other people’s answers survive their own admitted uncertainty.

Research applications

Audit checks of published research

Taking any counterforce result and asking whether the conclusion holds when the inputs are given the ranges their own sources publish. Lieber and Press’s survivor counts and Philippe and Stepanov’s fallout casualties are both under Sources. The force-sizing logic of the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) study group is named here as an example and is not cited: it has no entry. p(missy) is an instrument for doing exactly that.

The two-peer problem and force sizing debates

The core question is how many warheads are needed for two peers. That argument runs downstream of exchange arithmetic evaluated at point estimates. If the honest output is a distribution, then the requirement is a distribution too.

The question becomes how many warheads are needed to achieve what confidence of what outcome. That is a different question and a far more scrutable one. Uncertainty can mean you need more warheads, or it can mean the mission is unachievable at any number. Convexity pushes toward the second.

Prioritising measurement

p(missy) can tell you which unknowns are buying the most spread.

Take an illustration rather than a result: if reliability drove 60% of the output variance and yield 4%, the next research dollar would go to reliability. That is a Sobol decomposition, it is a small amount of work on top of what the model already does, and it converts p(missy) from a critique into a research agenda.

So, what changes?

Any published counterforce result can now be checked against the ranges its own sources admit to. Force sizing stops being a number and becomes a confidence level, which is a much harder question to hand-wave. And you can see which unknown is buying the most spread, so you know where the next research dollar goes. That last one is not built yet.

Does anything like this exist?

Not for exchange calculations. The sensitivity analysis tradition exists, and Kent and Thaler were doing something adjacent in 1989; both are named as precedent rather than cited, and neither is under Sources. Running the standard targeting chain over its own admitted input ranges and reporting the distribution is not in the open literature.

Frequently asked

Is this a targeting tool?

No. It reproduces published counterforce formulas in order to show how much of their output is decided by assumptions rather than by physics. Nothing in it is operational, and every formula in it is already in print.

Where do the numbers come from?

The blast and thermal formulas are from Glasstone and Dolan (1977). The lethal radius expressions, and the disagreement between them, are from Davis and Schilling (1973). The worked example the presets reproduce is from Lieber and Press (2017). Full citations are under Sources.

Which way does widening a range move the answer?

Usually towards more targets standing. The chance of a miss is raised to the number of warheads assigned to each target, and that function is convex in hardness, accuracy, reliability and yield, so the average across one of those ranges exceeds the value at the middle of it. The shape of the delivery error and the aiming bias bend the other way, and a range that is not centred on the value the slider sits at can move the answer either way on its own. The page reports the direction it actually found rather than asserting one.

Can I reproduce a result?

Yes, and there is nothing to remember in order to do it. Nothing on the model page is random: the ranges are integrated over a fixed lattice of points rather than sampled, so there is no seed and no run-to-run variation. Set the same inputs and the same numbers come back, to the last digit printed. Every point, and every setting that enters the exchange arithmetic, travels in the exported CSV.

Why is fire treated separately from blast?

Because the field treats it separately, which is the argument. The Fire tab runs from the same yield and the same burst height as the exchange calculation on the first two tabs, and no existing open tool reports both from one set of inputs.

Is any of this classified?

No. Every formula, table and figure used here is from the open literature, and each one is cited under Sources.

  12. Wellerstein, Alex. NUKEMAP. Stevens Institute of Technology, 2012–. nuclearsecrecy.com/nukemap.

    • Column 2 of the table under What current models miss on the About page. The effects model does carry atmospheric transmittance, but as a condition you select rather than a distribution it samples.

(missy)

A nuclear effects model that carries its uncertainty instead of rounding it off. The same inputs that set the odds of destroying a target also set how far the weapon starts fires, and both are computed here from one set of numbers.

Inputs

Equations, not one equation

Davis and Schilling print four readings of the same test data, entry 05 under Sources, and the three do not agree. The fourth is not a reading of hardness at all: it evaluates the pressure field and finds where it crosses the target hardness, so height of burst becomes an input instead of an assumption
Which formula to believe is itself an open question, so it is carried as one more dimension of the integral. Untick all four and the formula chosen above is used alone

Precisionhow carefully the ranges are covered, not what the answer says

NPoints across the ranges 4,096
—
This is the only control on the panel that does not change the answer. It changes how carefully the answer is worked out. The model has to average p(kill) over every combination of the ranges you have opened, and it does that by evaluating the calculation at this many points spread evenly through them. More points cost time and buy accuracy you cannot see at the digits printed; fewer are quicker and eventually start to wobble. 4,096 is the default because that is where the answer stops moving. The points are a fixed lattice rather than a random sample, so there is no seed: open this page tomorrow with the same settings and the same digits come back
One target

Everything else on this page is built out of this one function. It takes named inputs and returns one number. No sampling, no counting.

p(kill; H, σD, A| Y, n, HOB, ρf| σdr, σcr, b, ρ, q| τ, terrain, weather)
target hardness, damage function width, footprint weapon yield, warheads, height of burst, fuze delivery downrange and crossrange dispersion, bias, reliability, fratricide environment named, not modelled here — see Method

p(kill), written out in full

The rows above are the chain as it is actually evaluated, one step at a time. Written as a single expression, with every term this model carries left in rather than assumed away, it is the line below.

  p(kill) = 1 − ∏j=1n [ 1 − ρj · ∫0∞ D(max(0, r − A); LR, σD) · g(r; CEP, σdr/σcr, b)  dr ]

LR is the lethal radius, itself a function of the yield Y, the target hardness H, the yield exponent p, the height of burst and which of the four published expressions is being used. D is the damage function, a step at σD = 0 and a normal curve of width σD·LR above it, reading the miss distance less the target footprint A. g is the radial density of the impact point: circular at a shape of 1:1 with no bias, and the density of a displaced anisotropic normal otherwise. ρj is the reliability of the jth warhead, which is plain ρ for the first two and ρ(1 − q(1 − (1−ρ)j−2)) from the third, once fratricide q is switched on.

This is not how it is normally calculatedNo published treatment writes p(kill) this way, and this page does not evaluate it as one expression either — it runs the chain above step by step, which is the same arithmetic and far easier to check. The point of setting it down in one line is to show what a single reported kill probability is standing in for. In the usual form, six of the terms here are gone: the footprint is zero, the damage function is a step, the error is circular and unbiased, there is no fratricide, and the lethal radius comes from one formula rather than a choice of four. Every one of those is a decision, and none of them is usually written down.
What each input is worth

One bar per input. Each runs from the answer you get at one end of that input's range to the answer at the other, so the longest bar is the input your answer depends on most. The values under the ends of a bar are the input values that produce them, which is where the direction is: more accuracy pushes one way, a harder target the other. The ticks inside a bar are at equal steps of the input, so evenly spaced ticks mean an even trade and bunched ticks mean the middle of that range is not a fair summary of it.

Using this in research

The model is small on purpose. What it is for is taking a number somebody has published and asking what happens to it when the inputs are given as the ranges the sources themselves print.

  1. Reproduce the published number first. Set the controls to the assumptions the paper states and check the model returns its headline figure. The Lieber and Press rows under Checks are that test: their Table 1 gives 42, 13 and 8 surviving silos and this page returns 42, 13 and 8. If it does not reproduce, stop; nothing after this means anything.

  2. Widen each input to the span its own source gives. Not a span you invented — the one in the footnote. The published number will not move. A band will appear around it where there was none, and that band is the result.

  3. Read which input the band is made of. The bars under What each input is worth sort the inputs by how far each one moves the answer on its own. That ordering says which measurement would be worth arguing about and which would not, and it is usually not the one the literature argues about.

  4. Ask the planner's question, not the analyst's. The number a force-sizing argument needs is not the average. It is the chance that nothing survives, which is on the chart above and cannot be recovered from a mean and an error bar.

  5. Export and cite. The CSV carries every quadrature point and every setting that enters the exchange arithmetic. The point set is deterministic, so a result quoted from this page can be reproduced exactly by anyone who sets the same inputs.

Not yet, but nextA target list rather than a target count: a file with one row per aim point carrying its own hardness and footprint, and then the allocation problem, which is how to spread a fixed number of warheads across a fixed set of targets. After that, population and casualty figures, which is the same arithmetic reading a different column. Both are the reason this model is built around one target first.

Atmosphere

Meteorological visibility: the distance at which a large dark object against the horizon is just discernible. It is the one atmospheric number that is routinely measured and reported
min km
max km
Weather on the day is not a known quantity. G&D computes transmittance properly but for one condition only: a cloudless day with 12 miles of visibility, which is 19.3 km. Worth knowing about this span: it is probably an upper bound. In hazier air more light is scattered but much of it still arrives, so the total may not depend on visibility as strongly as the arithmetic here makes it (§7.14; rain, fog and dense haze are the exception at §7.15). Showing that would need the buildup factor to rise as visibility falls, and Fig. 7.98 is drawn for one visibility, so it cannot calibrate that. Held fixed here and flagged rather than guessed at
Fitted to G&D Fig. 7.98 at this burst height: —.
Light scattered out of the direct beam still arrives, and still ignites, so the effective path is shorter than the plain exponential assumes. G&D handles this with the curves at Fig. 7.98 rather than with a coefficient. This one used to be a guess; fitting the expression above to a digitisation of that figure gives about 2.1 at the surface, rising with burst height, which is the value the button sets (entry 06 under Sources). The fit is calibrated from 400 m up to 5 km, so at a surface burst the 2.1 is that fit extrapolated below its calibrated range rather than a fitted value. At B = 1 the formula counts only light that arrives without being scattered once, and its attenuation rate matches the coefficients G&D reserve for eye injury; for burns and ignition they count scattered light too (§7.95, §7.98).
