The three equations behind that number

Daniel asked to see these written out rather than described, so here they are, in the form Glasstone and Dolan give them.

1 Q(d) = f · Y4πd² · τ(d)

Radiant exposure at distance d, in calories per square centimetre. f is the fraction of the yield Y emitted as thermal radiation, and 4πd² is the surface of the sphere that energy has spread over by the time it arrives. G&D §7.101–7.102. Everything except τ is geometry.

2 τ(d) = exp(−3.912 · d / (V · B))

Atmospheric transmittance is the fraction of the fireball’s thermal radiation that survives the path to the target. Air scatters and absorbs light, and how much it does is what visibility measures: V is defined as the distance at which transmittance falls to 2%, and ln(0.02) = −3.912, which is where the constant comes from and is the whole of the derivation. So at one visibility distance 2% of the light is left, at half of it about 14%, at a quarter about 37%. B is a buildup factor: the plain exponential counts only light that reaches the target without being deflected once, and light scattered forward out of the beam still arrives and still ignites, so the effective path is longer than the geometric one. G&D handles this with the curves at Fig. 7.98 rather than with a coefficient, and B here stands in for them. It used to be the one number on this tab with no measured basis; fitting the expression above to a digitisation of that figure gives about 2.1 at the surface, rising with burst height, which is what the button beside the slider sets (entry 06 under Sources). The fit is good to about 6%, so it is an approximation to the figure rather than the figure, and it is calibrated from 400 m up to 5 km, so the surface value is an extrapolation of it.

3 Q(R) = Qign(material, Y)  →  solve for R

The ignition radius is the distance at which the exposure delivered equals the exposure that material needs. Qign is read from the tables below and depends on the yield as well as the material, because a larger weapon delivers the same energy over a longer pulse and more of it is lost to the surroundings while it arrives. There is no closed form for R once τ is in the way, so it is found numerically.

Glasstone and Dolan, Tables 7.35 and 7.40

Radiant exposure required for ignition, in calories per square centimetre, for materials exposed to a burst of the yield at the head of each column. Table 7.35 gives the thresholds themselves. Table 7.40 is the reason there are three columns rather than one: it is where G&D record that the threshold rises with yield, because the pulse from a larger weapon is longer and more heat is conducted away from the surface while it is still being delivered. Between the three tabulated yields this model interpolates on the logarithm of the yield, and below 35 kt and above 20 Mt it holds the end column rather than extrapolating.

Material 35 kt1.4 Mt20 Mt

What the tables do not give. The mix of these materials in a real city. Any uncertainty on the values themselves, which §7.36 calls "somewhat approximate" without saying by how much. Yields between the three columns. And any link at all from an ignition to a fire that spreads. That last gap is the largest one: nine pages on incendiary effects against 151 on blast.

Checked against what is in print

Every time this page loads it runs the calculation against figures already published, carried past the digit a briefing rounds them to. A block that is read off a source names the entry under Sources it comes from, so the row can be checked against the page it came from; the blocks that name no entry are arithmetic this model has to satisfy whatever the sources say, and they would catch an error no published figure would. Every row prints what it was allowed to differ by, because a verdict of match means nothing without it. Figures are carried in whatever unit their source printed, which is why metres, nautical miles and feet all turn up in one table, and it is why the model converts on the page rather than inside the arithmetic. If one of these rows says fail, something is wrong and nothing else here should be trusted.

What p(kill) is a function of

The published expressions take a handful of inputs. The list of things that actually bear on whether a warhead destroys a target is longer, and the difference between the two lists is most of what this model is about. Below is the whole list, grouped as it is grouped on the input panel, with what each term does and whether this page computes it. The same thing written as a single equation sits under the step-by-step chain on the One target tab.

On the five marked "named, not computed"Leaving a term out is a choice, and a choice that gets buried stops being visible as one. Each of the five is listed with what it would do to the answer, so that the size of the omission is on the page even though the term is not. They fail for three different reasons, which is worth separating. Burial geometry and terrain have no numeric basis anywhere in the open literature that I have found, and that absence is itself a finding. Transmittance and weather are computed, but on the Fire tab, and they do not feed back into the blast calculation because nothing published says how they should. The fuze reliability is the odd one out: it is perfectly well defined and it would change nothing here, because separating the fuze from the delivery chain only matters once reprogramming is modelled, and reprogramming is not. It is listed so that the reason it is absent is a stated reason rather than an oversight.
Every symbol on this page

The names, the units they are carried in, and in a few cases the thing the name hides.

Y kt
Yield. Every Davis and Schilling formula wants megatons, so 335 kt enters as 0.335. Brode and Small scale on kt1/3 and take kilotons directly.
H psi
Target hardness: the peak overpressure at which the target is counted as destroyed. 3,000 psi for a modern silo, which Lieber and Press state and bracket at roughly 2,000 to 3,000; 300 psi for a Minuteman silo as Davis and Schilling read it in 1973, and 900 after the hardening programme. The 2 to 5 psi quoted for launchers and houses is widely repeated and not traceable to anything cited here.
LR m
Lethal radius. The distance out to which the weapon produces the overpressure the target is rated to withstand. The three Davis and Schilling expressions return nautical miles, written nmi here, and the page converts at 1,852 m to the nautical mile.
A m
Target footprint, as an equivalent radius. Zero for a silo, which is a point. Not zero for an apron, a garrison or a dispersal area, where a warhead that lands anywhere on the footprint is on top of the target, so A comes off the miss distance before the damage function sees it. Under a cookie cutter that is the same as adding A to the lethal radius; with a damage function it is not, because the falloff belongs to the weapon and has no business widening with the apron.
CEP m
Circular error probable. The radius of the circle, centred on the aim point, that contains half the warheads. It is a median miss distance and a 50% containment radius, and it is neither a one-sigma figure nor a bound.
σdr, σcr m
Standard deviation of the impact point along the line of flight and across it. Equal only if the error really is circular. The pair is fixed by requiring that half the warheads land inside a circle of radius CEP, which is what CEP means. The familiar shortcut CEP ≈ 0.5887(σdr + σcr) is exact when the two are equal and drifts by about 2% at three to one, where it is furthest out, so the model solves the containment radius rather than using the shortcut.
b m
Bias: a systematic offset of the whole pattern from the target, from guidance calibration or from an error in the target's surveyed coordinates. Unlike CEP it does not average out over many shots, which is why it is carried separately.
σD dimensionless
Width of the damage function as a fraction of LR. 0 is the cookie cutter, 0.20 is Sigma-20.
Φ dimensionless
The cumulative distribution function of the standard normal: the share of a normal distribution lying below a given number of standard deviations. It is what makes the damage function a curve rather than a step.
SSPK dimensionless
Single shot probability of kill: the chance one warhead destroys the target, given that it arrives and goes off. It is the damage function averaged over where the warhead lands.
TKP dimensionless
Terminal kill probability: SSPK multiplied by reliability, so the chance one warhead assigned to the target both arrives and destroys it. p(miss) is one minus this.
ρ dimensionless
Overall reliability: the chance a warhead assigned to a target arrives and goes off. The product of the delivery chain and the fuze.
ρf dimensionless
The fuze's own share of that. Carried separately because a missile lost in boost and a warhead that arrives and duds are the same for the arithmetic here and different for anything that models reprogramming or fratricide.
q dimensionless
Fratricide: the chance an earlier burst takes out a later warhead aimed at the same target. Zero is the independent case every published formula assumes.
n, N counts
Warheads on one target, lower case. Targets in the set, upper case.
HOB m
Height of burst. Read only by Brode and Small; the other three have it assumed away at zero.
Every formula on this page

The lethal radius is the one quantity here with more than one published expression, and they do not agree. All of them are below, written as their sources write them, with what each is stated to be good for.

Where 2.62 comes from: it is not derived. Davis and Schilling take it off the General Electric Missile Effectiveness Calculator, a circular slide rule whose scale was fitted to Brode's 1960 test-shot data, and it is the branch of that fit stated for hardnesses above 1,000 psi. The other three coefficients on the panel are the other branches of the same slide rule.

The damage function

D(r) = Φ( (LR − r) / σDLR ). The chance the target is destroyed given a burst at distance r. At σD = 0 it is a step, which is the cookie cutter every lethal radius formula above assumes: certain death inside LR, untouched outside. At 0.20 it is the Sigma-20 function Davis and Schilling name in note 12 and then decline to use. Fitting the three points they print recovers a normal curve in radius with a standard deviation of 20% of the radius, which is what the name means.

Single shot probability of kill

SSPK = ∬ D(r) · g(r) dr, where g is the density of the miss distance. With a circular error and no bias g is Rayleigh with σ = CEP/1.1774 and the integral collapses, at σD = 0, to 1 − 0.5(LR/CEP)² exactly, which is the form Davis and Schilling print. With an elliptical error or a bias, g is the radial density of a displaced anisotropic normal and the integral is done numerically. Nothing has been replaced here, only extended: at 1:1 with no bias the code takes the circular path, which is the published closed form, and the checks confirm that path returns 1 − 0.5(LR/CEP)² to nine decimal places.

What CEP is, and is not

CEP is a containment radius. Draw a circle of that radius on the aim point and half of the warheads land inside it. That is the entire definition: a 50% localisation region, not a one-sigma figure and not a bound.

The confusion worth naming is with the familiar 68%. That figure belongs to one axis at a time, not to a circle. Under circular normal error CEP = 1.1774 σ, so the circle of radius one σ holds about 39% of shots, the circle of radius 1.1774 σ holds 50% by construction, and it takes a radius of about 1.55 σ — roughly 1.3 CEP — to reach 70%. About 21% of shots land beyond 1.5 CEP and about 2% beyond 2.4 CEP. That tail is doing real work here, because a target survives on the tail.

One more thing the C hides. The real error is an ellipse: warheads scatter further along the line of flight than across it, so the 50% region is longer than it is wide. Collapsing it to a circle is close enough when the target is small against the miss distance and wrong when it is not. Nothing in the open literature gives the ratio of the two axes for a deployed system, so rather than invent one the model makes it an input. CEP is held fixed as the shape changes: the two standard deviations are solved so that half the warheads still land inside a circle of the stated radius. Moving the control therefore redistributes a published accuracy figure rather than replacing it, and what you read off is the price of the assumption on its own.

From one warhead to n

TKP = SSPK · ρ, and with independent arrivals a target survives only if every warhead misses, so p(survive) = (1 − TKP)n. That exponent is why the middle of a range and the average across it give different answers, and why for hardness, accuracy, reliability and yield they differ in the same direction every time. The shape of the delivery error and the aiming bias bend the other way, so the direction is a property of the input rather than a rule. With fratricide switched on the arrivals are no longer independent and the product is taken term by term instead. Given p(survive), the number of survivors in a set of N is binomial and closed form; given a distribution over p(survive) it is that binomial averaged over the distribution, which is also closed form.

Why there is no Monte Carlo here

The question the ranges pose is an integral: average p(kill) over a box of inputs nobody knows exactly. The box runs to eleven dimensions at most — ten input spans and the choice of formula — and is seven at the defaults. An integral over a box like that is a quadrature problem, and drawing pseudorandom numbers is one of the worse ways to solve it — it converges as 1/√N and it makes the answer depend on a seed. This page uses a rank-1 lattice instead: a deterministic, evenly spread point set. On the six spans the defaults carry, measured against a reference run of 262,144 points, its error at 4,096 points is about twelve times below the average error of pseudorandom sets of the same size. That advantage narrows as more ranges are opened — about five times with all ten spans open, against about twelve at six — and would be gone before long, which is a known property of lattices built this way and is worth saying rather than glossing over; even there the lattice is no worse than sampling, and it still has no seed. The checks tab tests the point set itself — that it is identical on two calls, that it is equidistributed in every dimension, that it integrates a known integral, and that doubling the points does not move the answer — rather than repeating the comparison, which is too slow to run on every page load. The counting that follows the integral is closed form and is not approximated at all.

This matters beyond tidiness. A simulation invites the reading that the model is generating scenarios. It is not. It is evaluating one function over the range of inputs the literature actually supports, and reporting the range of answers that come out.

Fratricide

Warheads aimed at one target arrive three to five seconds apart, and a burst throws up debris that persists for six to eight seconds, so a warhead is at risk from its own side only once one has gone off ahead of it with time to spare, which is from the third arrival onward. Writing q for the chance an earlier burst takes out a later warhead, a warhead two or more places behind a burst arrives with probability ρ(1 − q) rather than ρ.

The arrivals are then not independent, so p(survive) is not a product of per-warhead terms: a warhead is at risk only if an earlier one actually went off, and that same earlier burst had its own shot at the target. Conditioning on which warhead arrives first removes the dependence, because after that every later warhead faces the same debris, and summing over that first index is exact. At q = 0 it collapses to (1 − TKP)n, which is one of the rows under Checks. Lieber, Press and Chipman put q near 0.75.

It is the one correction on this page that runs against the attacker rather than for him, which is why it is worth having next to the ones that run the other way. It is also the crudest thing here: the timings say the immediately preceding burst is the dangerous one, and this treats every burst two or more places back as equally dangerous with no decay. What the problem really wants is a timing model rather than a coefficient.

What is computed, and what is assumed

Worth keeping straight, because the two get confused and only one of them is a result.

Computed

The lethal radius, from the yield and the target hardness. The chance one warhead kills the target, from that radius, the accuracy, the shape of the error and any bias. The chance the target survives n warheads, with or without fratricide. The number of survivors across a field, and the whole distribution of possible numbers including the chance that none survive. All of it from the formulas on this tab. Two numbers in it are fits rather than published values — the Sigma-20 width, reconstructed from three printed points, and the forward-scatter buildup factor — and the parameters with no published basis at all are marked in gold.

Assumed

That every warhead aimed at a target arrives independently, unless fratricide is switched on. That the attacker does not re-fire at targets he can see he missed, which he would, and which would raise his result. That the target's failure mode is peak overpressure alone, when a buried structure can also be reached through the soil. That weather is the same everywhere. Each of these is a choice, and the ones that push in the attacker's favour are listed below so nobody has to guess which way the model leans.

What these formulas do not do

Scaffold, not a finding. Parameters marked with a gold mark have no measured basis. One target here is one aim point, not one warhead: a surviving silo may hold a MIRVed missile carrying several, so surviving targets is a floor on surviving warheads rather than a count of them. That error runs the same direction the convexity does, toward understating what is left to retaliate with.

Davis and Schilling record that two corrections pull opposite ways and, for the weapons in their own example, roughly cancel: the pulse duration adjustment raises kill probability and the damage function lowers it. Both are on this page, the first as the yield exponent and the second as σD, so that pair is no longer half-counted. What is still missing runs the other way. Reprogramming, which Davis and Schilling model in detail, is not here, and it raises kill probability by letting the attacker replace the missiles he watches fail. Neither is height of burst optimised: the checks show that against a 3,000 psi silo the best burst height reaches 9.5% further than the surface burst every formula here assumes, and further still as the target gets harder. An attacker who optimises height does better than this page reports.

On the fire side, transmittance is Beer–Lambert on the slant distance with a scatter buildup term fitted to G&D Fig. 7.98, which reproduces that figure to within about 6% and is not the figure itself. Ignition thresholds are log-interpolated on yield between the three tabulated columns. The thermal fraction is still a two-way switch between a surface burst and an air burst; G&D tabulate it for the heights in between at Table 7.101, and that interpolation is not here yet, which makes burst height matter less to the fire answer than it should. Also not included: secondary ignitions from blast damage, smoke shielding the pulse from what is behind it, terrain and structure shielding in three dimensions, fire spread, fallout.

And the largest one of all, which is not a missing coefficient but a missing connection: nothing here turns a count of ignitions into a fire, or a fire into soot in the stratosphere. That chain is where the nuclear winter literature begins and where the targeting literature has already stopped.

By Madeline Berzak
